column2: Q11: "Does turning up the music in a bar cause people to drink more beer?"

column1: #   "Sound level of environmental music and drinking behavior: A field experiment with
# Design (naturalistic field experiment): 40 male beer drinkers (aged 18-25) observed
#   in 2 bars in western France over 3 Saturday nights; the bars' usual top-40 music
#   was randomly set to the normal level (72 dB) or a high level (88 dB). Outcomes
#   observed per patron: number of beer glasses ordered and time spent drinking a glass.
# Published headline results (paper abstract; Reuters / HealthDay / Daily Star
#   coverage of the July 2008 study): loud music increased the mean number of drinks

column3: and cut the mean time to drink a glass

column1: #   14.51 -> 11.45 minutes (about 3 minutes faster). Both differences significant.
# Lock5 3e ships no dataset for this question (checked lock5stat.com/datapage3e.html;
#   the only "beer" match there is PumpkinBeer
# No public microdata exists for this study. Rows below are a documented
#   reconstruction from the published group means:
#   - n = 20 patrons per condition: the 40 patrons were randomly assigned to the two
#     sound levels; the exact split is not published
#   - glasses (integer counts) and time_per_glass_min (minutes) are reconstructed to
#     reproduce the published condition means exactly (normal: 2.6 glasses and
#   - Per-patron spread is NOT published. The reconstructed SDs (glasses ~0.82 vs
#     ~0.88; time ~2.3 vs ~1.5 min) are documented assumptions chosen to be plausible
#     for bar patrons. Test statistics below therefore illustrate the Lock5 method on
#     the published means rather than exactly reproducing the paper's inferential
#     statistics (the paper reports significant differences in both outcomes).
#          glasses = number of beer glasses ordered during the observation;
#          time_per_glass_min = average minutes the patron took to drink one glass.
